title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: Shiva calls the world an illusion, food and all, so Parvati vanishes, and the kitchens of the world go empty
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth of Durga's sister goddesses, Parvati, outlasted Shiva at austerity and turned her back on his mockery, until he dropped the disguise. Did you stand by something you love? Day one thousand eighty.

On Kailash, an argument. Shiva, the great ascetic, is explaining that the world of things is illusion, maya. Bodies, houses, possessions, even food: none of it is ultimately real. Parvati listens. And then, in the story people tell, she decides to let him find out what that means. She disappears. And with her goes every grain, every loaf, every pot on every stove. The fields stand empty. Creatures go hungry. Even the gods grow faint. Even Shiva. Today, Parvati again, and an argument made without a single word.
screen: `SHIVA: EVEN FOOD IS ILLUSION.` → `PARVATI DISAPPEARS.` → `EVERY KITCHEN GOES EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Word comes that somewhere in the world, food is still being served. In Kashi, the holy city of Varanasi, a kitchen is open. And at its door stands a goddess with a ladle and a pot that never runs out. She feeds everyone who comes. Her name, in this story, is Annapurna, and tradition explains it as the one who is full of food. So Shiva, lord of the universe, the great ascetic who said food was unreal, walks to Kashi with a begging bowl, and holds it out to her. And she fills it. The images of this moment are tender, not triumphant: the goddess serving, the god receiving, a family meal. Some tellers say Shiva learned that the body and its hunger are not to be waved away; some say that Parvati wasn't arguing against his teaching at all, but filling it out. In that reading, spirit needs a body to live in, and a body needs to eat. In Varanasi a temple to Annapurna stands near Shiva's own, and devotees speak of her as the mother who makes sure no one in the city goes hungry. And with that, the five are met: the warrior, the fierce mother, the one who chooses, the hidden river, and now the cook at the door in Kashi, filling Shiva's bowl. Five characters. And some Hindus would add, one power moving through all of them. That's tomorrow's question.
screen: `A KITCHEN STILL OPEN IN KASHI.` · `ANNAPURNA, THE ONE FULL OF FOOD.` · `SHIVA HOLDS OUT A BEGGING BOWL.` · then, large: `SHE FILLS IT.` · then: `FIVE CHARACTERS, MET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor the food. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the last thing you ate. Trace it back: who cooked it, who carried it, who grew it, the rain, the soil. Let the chain be long. Notice the body that received it, and is using it right now to breathe. If you pray, you can thank Annapurna or God for food in your own words. If you don't, just thank the hands. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name over all five goddesses met in this run; today, the Goddess as Annapurna, filling Shiva's bowl. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, before you eat, pause long enough to notice whose hands it passed through. Tomorrow, Shakti as a philosophy. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Annapurna is honored in homes and kitchens as the goddess of nourishment, and her temple in Varanasi stands near the Kashi Vishwanath temple of Shiva; some families offer a little food to her before a meal.

go to Kashi and hold out a begging bowl

original.note: Sanskrit: Annapurna; tradition explains the name as 'she who is full of food,' and knows her as a form of Parvati.

trapdoor: what you thought: Annapurna is a separate kitchen goddess.
what it means: in the story she's Parvati, who withdraws food to show that the body and its hunger matter, then feeds Shiva himself.
what a scholar hears: the scene pairs Shiva as Bhikshatana, the beggar, with Annapurna, and Varanasi keeps both in its temples.

notes: The maya argument and Parvati's disappearance are told as 'the story people tell'; versions vary and its textual basis is mainly popular. Keeper to confirm the retelling and whether citing the Kashi Khanda is appropriate.
Annapurna as 'the one full of food' is attributed to tradition (anna + purna); confirm.
'A temple to Annapurna stands near Shiva's own' (Annapurna temple near Kashi Vishwanath) is a location claim; confirm.
Scholar floor mentions Shiva as Bhikshatana in connection with Annapurna; confirm this association is fair.
